caseno: Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11847 of 2008 and Case No. 4985 of 2009.
lawyer:
Anisul Huq with Sk Baharul Islam, Advocates—For the Petitioner. (In Criminal Misc. Case No. 4985 of 2009) 
Md Ziaul Hoque, Advocate—For the Petitioner. (In Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11847 of 2008). 
Md Jashimuddin, Assistant Attorney-General and Shah Abdul Hatem, Assistant Attorney-General—For the State-opposite-Party No. 1. (In both the cases). 
Kamal-ul-Alam with Shaikh Azmol Hayat, Advocates—For the Complainant-opposite-Party No. 2. (In both the cases).
parties:
Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed and others------Petitioner
VS
State and another------Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Md Nazrul Islam Talukder J: These Rules, at the instance of two accused-petitioners, were issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the impugned proceedings of CR Case No. 121 (Kotwali Zone) of 2007 under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, now pending in the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong should not be quashed and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. Since both the Rules have arisen from the same CR Case and the common questions of laws and facts are involved in these Rules, they are heard together and agreeing disposed of by this analogous judgment. 

 On 27-2-2007, one Nur Mohammad on behalf of the Islam Steel Mills Limited as complainant instituted a petition of complaint before the Court of Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong against the accused-petitioners alleging, interline, that as per contract, the complainant agreed to supply different types of MS rod to the petitioners for construction of a building of the Hospital. For the purpose of construction of the building, an work order was issued in favour of the Islam Steel Mills Limited on 5-3-2003. The contract was valued at Taka 1,33,20,000 out of which the petitioners paid Taka 60,00,000 (sixty lakh); but an amount of taka 73,30,000 (seventy three lakh thirty thousand) remained unpaid. The complainant requested the accused-petitioner to pay up the out-standing demand as a result the accused-petitioners, on behalf of the company, issued 4(four) cheques dated 30-8-2006, 7-9-2006, 15-9-2006 and 22-9-2006 for an amount of Taka 73,00,000 (seventy three lakh). On receipt of the aforesaid cheques, the complainant presented the aforesaid cheques to the Agrani Bank, Laldighi Eastern Branch, Chittagong; but those were bounced for insufficient fund. The complainant asked for the cheque-amount to the accused-petitioners over telephone; but the accused-petitioners informed that the processes of the encashment of the cheques were being made. On the basis of the statement made by the accused-petitioners, the complainant again presented the cheques before Agrani Bank, Laldighi Eastern Branch, Chittagong on 17-1-2007; but the said cheques were again dishonored and returned unpaid for insufficient fund. Subsequently, after bouncing of the cheques, the complainant issued a legal notice upon accused Nos. 1-3 for payment of cheque-amount; but they did not pay any heed to the demand of the complainant. On 21-1-2007, an Estate-Officer of the complainant's company went to the office of the accused-petitioner's company for taking the payment of the cheque-amount; but they denied payment of the same. Thereafter, the complainant issued a legal notice through his Advocate upon accused Nos. 1-3 on 28-1-2007 for payment of an amount of taka 73,00,000 within 30 days from the date of receipt of the legal notice. After expiry of 26 days from the date of receipt of the legal notice, the accused-petitioners did not take any step for payment of the cheque-amount. Accused Nos. 1 and 2 are the Directors of the company and they issued the cheques. Accused No. 3 is also a director who issued the work order and accused No. 4 is the owner and chairman of the company namely Ibrahim Iqbal Memorial Hospital Limited. Since no payment against the cheques was made within the stipulated period mentioned in the legal notice, the complainant filed this instant case on 27-2-2007 against the accused-petitioners under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 after complying with all the requirements of law. Hence, this case against the accused-petitioners under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 

 4. It appears from the record of the case that the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed in Criminal Miscellaneous Case. No. 4895 of 2009 approached this Court with an application for anticipatory bail whereupon this Court, by an order dated 10-8-2008, enlarged the accused-petitioner on anticipatory bail till framing of the charge. The accused-petitioner Zahidul Islam Jahangir in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11847/08 also obtained bail from the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate on 13-7-2007. The Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Court No. 3, Chittagong, by an order dated 27-2-2007, took cognizance of the offences against both the accused-petitioners and 2 others under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. It transpires from the record that no charge has been framed against the accused-petitioners under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 

 6. At the very outset, Mr Anisul Huq, learned Advocate along with Mr Sk Baharul Islam, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 4985 of 2009, submits that legal notice required under section 138. of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 for payment on the cheque-amount was issued upon accused Nos. 1-3 on 28-1-2007 and they received the same on 1-2-2007; but the act remains that no notice was served upon the accused-petitioner for payment of the cheque-amount and in such a posture of things, the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is not maintainable and sustainable in the eye of law and in that view of the matter, the impugned proceedings should be quashed. He next submits that in view of the provisions contemplated by section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, notice is to be served on the drawer demanding payment of the cheque amount within 30 days from the date of receipt of legal notice and if the payment against the cheque amount is not made within the given period of 30 days, the complainant is authorized by law to file a petition of complaint against the accused within next one month from the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138 of the Act. He then submits that in the instant case, the notice was alleged to have been received by accused Nos. 1-3 on 1-2-2007 and the case of action would have arisen on 1-3-2007 but the petition of complaint was filed before the Court on 27-2-2007, that is, before arising of the cause of action and in that view of the matter, the impugned proceedings filed before expiry of 30 days from the date on which the cause of action arises is not tenable and sustainable in the eye of law. Learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the decisions decided in the cases of SM Anwar Hossain vs Shafiul Alam (Chand), 4 BLC (AD) 106 and Jubayer vs State 15 BLC 432. He lastly submits that since the company has not been made accused in the instant case, the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed are not maintainable and, as such, the impugned proceedings being abuse of the process of the Court should be quashed. 

 7. Mr Mohammed Ziaul Hoque, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioner Zahidul Islam Jahangir in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11847 of 2008, by referring to supplementary affidavit dated 8-3-2011 field by the accused-petitioner, submits that the complainant earlier served a legal notice upon the accused on 7-12-2006; but no proceeding was started against the accused from that point of time; rather he issued 2nd notice on 28-1-2007 and filed the impugned case against the accused suppressing the fact of issuance of earlier legal notice upon him and from this stand-point, the impugned proceedings are barred from the first notice and, as such, it should be quashed. Learned Advocate, in support of his submission, has relied on the decisions laid down in the cases of Mrs LP Christiat vs Ch, Suryanarayana reported. in Criminal Law Journal (2007) 2010 and Dr Md Mofizur Rahman vs Md Bashrullah 55 DLR 630. He next submits that no notice was served upon the company as well as upon the proper representative of the company and that section 141 of the Act provides the procedure for taking cognizance of the offence under section 138 of the Act within one month from the date of cause of action; but in the instant case, the cognizance of the alleged offence was taken before arising of the cause action, which is illegal and on that ground, the impugned proceedings being abuse of process of the Court should be quashed. Learned Advocate, in support of his contention, has banked on the decision in the case of Jubayer vs State, 15 BLC 432. 

 8. On the other hand, Mr Kamal-ul-Alam, learned Advocate along with Mr Shaikh Azmol Hayat, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite-party No. 2 in both the miscellaneous cases, submits that all the Directors and the chairman of the company have been implicated as accused in the instant case and that notice was served upon accused Nos. 1-3 and, as such, service of notice upon the three Directors amounts to service of notice upon the company and in that view of the matter, it cannot be said that notice was no served upon the company and the proper representative of the company and in this perspective, the impugned proceedings brought against the accused-petitioners should not be quashed. He next submits that though the instant case was filed before the expiry of 33 days from the date of cause of action, the impugned proceedings should not be quashed. Learned Advocate,. in support of his submission, has adverted to the decisions spelt out in the cases of Jamir Uddin vs SM Safi reported in 16 BLC 577, Sanwar Hossain Moni vs State reported in 16 BLC (AD) 71, Nurun Nabi vs State reported in 17 BLC 340. He next submits that if the person committing an offence under section 138 is a Company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to, the Company for the conduct of the business of the Company as well as. the Company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and under the given .context of law, the impugned proceedings initiated against the petitioners should not be quashed. He then submits that. the accused Nos. 1-3 are the Directors and accused No. 4 is. the owner and chairman of the company and that the alleged offence has been committed with the consent and connivance of all the accused and this being the state of affairs, the petitioners may be deemed to be guilty to the offences and they should be proceeded against. He lastly submits that admittedly notices were served upon the three Directors of the company and, as such, it is deemed to have been served upon the company as well as upon the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed. The learned Advocate, in support of his contention, has relied on the decision taken in the case of Md Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs State reported in 18 BLT 90 and considering that aspects of the case, the impugned proceedings should not be quashed. 

 11. Now, the pertinent question arises as to whether the impugned proceeding is liable to be quashed or not. To decide this issue, it will be necessary to see the extent of principles and categories of cases in which High Court Division may invoke its extra-ordinary power and authority under section 561A of the Code of criminal Procedure for quashing a proceeding. 

 12. In the case of Abdul Quader Chowdhury vs State, 28 DLR (AD) 38, it has been spelt out that to bring a case within the purview of section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the purpose of quashing a proceeding, one of the following conditions must be fulfilled: 

 (1) Interference even at an initial stage may be justified where the facts are so preposterous that even on admitted facts no case stands against the accused. 

 (4) In a case where the allegations in the FIR or the petition of complaint, even if taken at their face value and accepted in their entirety, do not constitute the offence as alleged. 

 (5) The allegations against the accused although constitute an offence alleged but there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case or the evidence adduced clearly or manifestly fails to prove the charge. 

 13. Similar view of the principles of quashing the proceedings was, subsequently, followed in the decision laid down in the case of Ali Akkas vs Enayet Hossain, 17 BLD (AD) (1997) 44 = 2 BLC (AD) 16. 

 14. It is pertinent to note that the inherent power under section 561A of the Code of criminal Procedure can be invoked at any stage of the proceeding even after conclusion of the trial, if it is necessary to prevent the abuse of the process of the court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. In the case of Sher Ali vs State, 46 DLR (AD) 67 it has been decided :— 

 15. Coming back to the present case, it appears that the accused Nos. 1 and 2 issued 4 cheques in faovur of the complainant for pay up the outstanding dues. We have found that all the cheques were dishonoured for insufficient fund. The complainant thereafter issued legal notice upon the accused Nos. 1-3 for payment of the cheque amount but they denied payment of the cheque-amount in time and thereafter the complainant filed the instant case against the accused-petitioners and others under sections 138 /140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. In the case of Monzur Alam vs State reported in 55 DLR (AD) 62, it has been held :— 

 17. From the above facts and circumstances of the case, there is evidently a prima-facie case in the petition of complaint to proceed against the accused-petitioners under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 

 18. Now another question arises for consideration. Learned Advocate Mr Anisul Huq appearing on behalf of the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed, points out that admittedly, cheques were issued by accused Nos. 1 and 2, and accused. No. 3 issued the work order, but accused No. 4 is no way connected with the affairs of the instant case. Furthermore, no notice was served on him asking for making payment of the cheque amount within 30 days from the date of receipt of the legal notice and, as such, there is no cause of action for filing of the instant case against the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed. 

 20. It appears from section 138 of the Act that notices for payment of the cheque amount are to be served on the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid. It clearly appears that there is no provision to serve notice upon the person who did not, issue any cheque in favour of the complainant of the case. Admittedly, cheques were issued by accused Nos. 1 and 2 and accused No. 3 issued the work order. We find that the notices were served upon accused Nos. 1-3. In view of the provision available in section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the requirement of law for service of notice upon the drawer of the cheque has been complied with. From the averments made in the petition of complaint, it appears that accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed is the chairman of Ibrahim Iqbal Memorial Hospital Limited on whose behalf the cheques were issued by the two Directors, the accused Nos. 1 and 2. section 140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act provides that if the person committing an offence under section 138 is a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of and was responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. Since the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed is the chairman of the company, he has been made accused in the instant case properly section 140 of the Act further contemplates that where any offence under this Act has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of or is attributable to, any neglect on the part of any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. Since the accused-petitioners are Directors and chairman of the company, they are necessary parties in the instant case as per section 140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. Pursuant to the allegations made in the petition of complaint, the accused-petitioners have been made accused in the case. It is stated earlier that notice for payment of the cheque amount may only be served on the drawer of the cheque in view of section 138 (b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act and there is no provision of law to issue separate notice on the person who is not drawer of the cheque. In the instant case the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed is not the drawer of the cheque and, as such, no separate notice demanding cheque amount under section 138(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 is necessary. Since the allegation brought in the petition of complaint indicates that the accused, in collaboration with each other, issued the cheque and work order as well, they are prima facie held responsible for the offences under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. Under the circumstances the accused-petitioners have been impleaded as accused in the instant case in accordance with law. 

 21. In this regard, learned Advocate for opposite-party No.2 has referred to a decision taken in the case of Md Habibur Rahman Chowdhury vs State reported in 18 BLT 90 wherein it has been decided:- 

 "It also appears that the accused-petitioner as managing director of the Company was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business. Thus he was responsible for bouncing the Asia cheques and thereby committed the offence punishable under section 138 of the Act. Since the accused-petitioner was responsible for the offence alleged, the company, M/s. MS Refinery Ltd need not be made accused in the case pursuant to section 140(1) of the Act." 

 22. Since all the Directors of the company have been made accused in the instant case and since the company is represented by them, there is no necessity to implead the company separately as accused in the instant case. As the notice was served on the Directors of the company, it will be deemed that notice has been served upon the company itself. Under the circumstances, we are of the view that the impugned proceeding brought against the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin  Ahmed in criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 4985 of 2009 and others is maintainable in the eye of law and in that count, the impugned proceedings cannot be quashed and in this regard, the submissions made by the learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed do not hold good and the same fall through. Accordingly, the decisions referred to by the learned advocate for the petitioner Engineer Afsaruddin Ahmed are not applicable to the present case. 

 23. Another point raised by Mr Md Ziaul Hoque, learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner Zahidul Islam Jahangir in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11847 of 2008 is that since no allegation has been levelled against the accused No. 3 in the petition of complaint, the proceedings initiated against him are not tenable in the eye of law. In order to address the said ground, we have gone through the entire petition of complainant. It appears from the paragraph No. 3 of the petition of complaint that all the accused of the case are owner and Directors of the company and the accused Nos. 1 and 2 as Directors issued cheques on behalf of the company and accused No. 3 as director also issued the work order on behalf of the company. It also appears from the petition of complaint that the accused No. 4 is the owner and chairman of the company. Since allegation has been levelled against them in the petition of complaint to the effect that the accused-petitioners, in collaboration with each other, issued the cheque and issued the work order and did not arrange payment for the dis honoured cheques, a prima facie case has been disclosed against them in the petition of complainant. Learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner Zahidul Islam Jahangir, in support of his submission, has also referred to a decision is the case of AKM Siddique vs Md Momenul Haque reported in 11 BLC 454 wherein it has been laid down :— 

 24. In order to come to a decision, we have gone through the relevant prosecution materials wherefrom we have found that the accused, in collaboration with each other, issued the cheques and they are prima facie responsible for non-payment of the cheque amount in favour of the complainant. Whether the accused-petitioners were responsible for non-payment of money is a disputed question of fact, which is a matter of trial and evidence, and the same may, be gone into during trial of the case. Since the petition of complaint prima-facie discloses offences against the accused-petitioner and others under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, those allegations cannot be brushed aside at this stage and the same can only be resolved and decided on taking evidence of the respective parties. 

 25. Learned Advocate for the accused-petitioner Zahidul Islam Jahangir in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No. 11847 of 2008, by referring to supplementary affidavit dated 8-3-2011 filed by the accused-petitioner, further points out that since legal notice demanding payment was issued earlier on 7-12-2006 against dishonour of cheques, the case ought to have been filed before the Court counting period of time from the said first notice issued on 7-12-2006 and since the 2nd notice was issued on 28-1-2007, the impugned proceedings filed by the complainant is barred by law. It is further contended by him that since the complainant suppressed the fact of first notice in the petition of complaint, the impugned proceedings filed by the complainant against the accused-petitioners are liable to be quashed for suppression of fact. In this regard, the learned Advocate has referred to a decision taken in the case of Mrs LP Christiat vs Ch. Suryanaroyana reported in Criminal Law Journal (2007) 20W wherein it has been spelt out in paragraph No. 14:— 

 "In the present facts and circumstances of the case and keeping in view the provisions of the Act, I have no hesitation to hold that the suppression of facts as to the presentation of the cheque and issuance of statutory legal notice on an earlier occasion amounts to draw an inference that there are no bonafides on the part of the complainant in approaching this Court by violating the provisions of the act" 

 26. Though the learned Advocate Mr Mohammed Ziaul Hoque points out about two notices from the supplementary affidavit dated 8-3-2011 filed by the accused-petitioner Zahidul Islam Jahangir the aforesaid fact has not been stated in the petition of complaint. We do not find such averments in the petition of complaint and, as such, it is not an admitted fact to be relied upon. It is a settled principle of law that the disputed question of fact cannot be decided by this Court sitting in its extra-ordinary jurisdiction under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Under the circumstances, the accused-petitioners have the ample opportunity to agitate the point before the trial Court during trial of the case and the complainant is also at liberty to cross-examine the prosecution witnesses to disprove the allegation about service of a previous notice allegedly issued upon accused Nos. 1-3. 

 27. From the facts and circumstances of the case, the decisions adverted to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner Zahidul Islam Jahangir do not appear to be applicable to the instant case. 

 29. Coming back to the present case, it appears from the petition of complaint that the accused Nos. 1 and 2 issued 4 (four) cheques in favour of complainant-opposite party No. 2 who, in due course of time, presented the same before the bank for encashment; but those were dishonoured for insufficient funds. After bouncing of the cheques, the complainant issued legal notices upon the accused Nos. 1-3, who avoided payment of the cheque amounts inspite of legal notice served by the complainant. It may be pointed out that the complainant issued a legal notice upon accused Nos. 1-3 on 28-1-2007 requesting them to pay up the cheque-amounts and the accused Nos. 1- 3 received the same on 1-2-2007; but the complainant filed the petition of complaint on 27-2-2007. Against this backdrop, the learned advocates for the petitioners contend that the impugned proceeding is a premature one and given this context, the impugned proceedings should be quashed. 

 Section 138(b)—"the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid." 

 Section 138(c)—"the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of the said notice." 

 33. In order to substantiate the submission, the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 2, has relied upon a decision in the case of Sarwar Hossain Moni vs State reported in 16 BLC (AD) 71, wherein it has been held :— 

 34. In the decision made in the case of Satya Narayan Poddar vs State reported in 53 DLR 403 relied upon by the learned Advocate for the opposite-party No. 2, it has been laid down :— 

 "Even though the case is pre-mature and it was filed before the expiry of 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice, the proceeding is not liable to be quashed." 

 35. In the decision decided in the case of Sirajul Islam vs Tauhid Uddin Ahmed reported in 15 BLC 39 adverted to by the learned Advocate for opposite-party No. 2, it has been decided :— 

 "In the instant case, the complaint was filed before the statutory period. The accused-petitioner did not make any payment of the amount of the cheque after the receipt of the notice nor did he take any step to make payment of the said amount in the subsequent time which clearly shows that the accused-petitioner had no intention to make the payment of the said amount. Considering this fact of the matter, it cannot be said that the legal right of the accused petitioner had been infringed." 

 36. Under the given scenario of the case, we should consider the legislative import and intent of enactment of law regarding bouncing of the cheque. 

 37. The purpose and object of enactment of law is to combat and prevent the offences disclosed in the enacted law. In order to find out the import and intent of the enactment, the provisions of the Act should be interpreted in such a way and manner in keeping with the intention of the Legislature so that the law can adequately serve the purposes and effectively deals with the offences. It should be borne in mind that the substantive justice should not be frustrated or otherwise defeated for any technicality in the law. It is evident from the petitions of complaint that the accused Nos. 1 and 2 issued 4 (four) cheques in favour of the complainant who, in due course, presented the same for encashment; but those were bounced. The complainant issued legal notices upon the accused Nos. 1-3, who denied payment of the cheque amount. The complainant thereafter, filed the petitions of complaint before the competent court having jurisdiction. It may be mentioned here that the accused-petitioner even after filing of petition of complaint and after expiry of statutory period, did not make any payment of the cheque amount; rather the accused-petitioners appeared in the proceedings and on being enlarged on bail, they did not take any step for payment of the cheque amount. Under the circumstances, it can be easily presumed that had the accused-petitioners the intention to pay off the cheque amount, they could have done so subsequently, but they conspicuously remained silent about the payment of the cheque amount. In the decision taken in the case of Satya Narayan Poddar vs State reported in 53 DLR (2001) 403, it has been held that though the petition of complaint was filed before the expiry of 30 days from the date of receipt of legal notice, the impugned proceedings are not liable to be quashed on the ground of pre-maturity of the cause of action. The aforesaid legal view has been subsequently, endorsed by the Appellate Division in the decision in the case of Sarwar Hossain Mont vs State reported in 16 BLC (AD) 71, wherein it has been decided to the effect that a proceeding can not be quashed on the ground of pre-maturity of the cause of action, even if the petition  of complaint was filed before the expiry of 30 days from the date of the cause of action. 

 39. Considering the facts and circumstances of the case and the propositions of law discussed above, we are of the view that the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioners under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments act, 1881 cannot be circumvented merely on the fact that the petition of complaint was field before the expiry of 30 days from the date on which the cause of action arises under clause (c) of the proviso to section 138 of the Act. 

 40. From the foregoing discussions and regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case, we are led to hold that the impugned proceedings initiated against the accused-petitioners under sections 138/140 of the Negotiable Instruments act, 1881 cannot be quashed and that the same are maintainable and sustainable in the eye of law. 

 41. Having considered all the aspects of the case, we do not find merit in these Rules. Accordingly, both the Rules fail. 

 43. The orders of stay passed in both the criminal miscellaneous cases at the time of issuance of the rules stand vacated. 

 44. The learned Judge of the trial Court is directed to proceed with the case in accordance with law.
